_slice.why: S2's spec block is a whole page, so it carries about ninety card-internal rules that belong to S2b. DROPPED is enforced for this spec only once S2b is actually in the tree.

facts.means: the card sheet is APPLIED, by whichever of the two files imports it. Not 'the file exists': it was committed inert first so the transcription could be reviewed before it could move a pixel. The second spelling is the one that shipped - S2b's import landed in Shell.tsx, not page.tsx, and the single-file version of this fact read false on the very tree it exists to detect.
the page renders the shell, which is what makes the shell's import reach THIS page. Without it the branch above would accept a sheet imported by a shell nobody renders.

.m-dir.why: THE MASCOT'S INNER DOM IS THE `page-mascot` PACKAGE'S, NOT OURS. The design draws the fox from its own markup and we render <Mascot/> from the package, which ships its own structure and styling. Transcribing these would be a second, competing description of a DOM we do not author, and the first time the package changed its internals ours would point at elements that no longer exist. The rendered result is checked by scripts/mascot-check.mjs instead of the rules behind it.

.stage .tag.why:
RE-SCOPED TO OUTRANK globals.css, AND IT ADDS ONE DECLARATION, NAMED. The re-scoping is as above - one ancestor, so it outranks the legacy sheet. What it adds beyond the design's body is:
  text-transform:none
which closes globals.css:151-155 `.tag { ... text-transform: uppercase; ... }`. The legacy sheet upper-cases every tag at the same (0,1,0) specificity as the design's own `.tag`, so source order decided it and the design's tags shipped shouting. #575's review could not see it because `.tag` matched zero elements on that tree - the chips arrive with these views.
Named per the CTO's round-three ruling: an `override` whose body adds to the spec's names each addition and the globals.css rule it closes, or it is a `divergence`. Round three pasted "SAME DECLARATIONS" onto this entry and it was false - the checker's own sameBodies says so.

.stage ::selection.why:
RE-SCOPED TO OUTRANK globals.css, AND IT ADDS ONE DECLARATION, NAMED. The re-scoping is as above - one ancestor, so it outranks the legacy sheet. What it adds beyond the design's body is:

which closes globals.css:101 `::selection { background: color-mix(in srgb, var(--color-accent) 30%, transparent); }`. Same shape, different token: globals highlights selected text in the RETIRED accent. `.stage ::selection` is (0,1,1) against globals' (0,0,1), so this is specificity rather than order.
Named per the CTO's round-three ruling: an `override` whose body adds to the spec's names each addition and the globals.css rule it closes, or it is a `divergence`. Round three pasted "SAME DECLARATIONS" onto this entry and it was false - the checker's own sameBodies says so.

.tag.more.why: RE-SCOPED TO OUTRANK globals.css, SAME DECLARATIONS (#575). The legacy sheet styles the same element at the same specificity, so the design's own selector loses on source order alone. One ancestor is added - `html` for element rules, `.stage` for page furniture - which raises specificity without changing what is painted. The spec's key and ours therefore differ while the CSS does not, which the checker reports as one dropped rule plus one added rule: the same divergence twice.

.tip.why: A GAP, NOT A DECISION, and it is declared here only so the gate can measure the other two hundred rules. The design's drips chart carries a hover tooltip (shell.css:287, index.html:637) and we ship neither the rule nor the element. Filed as #594 against the sheet owner. When it ships, this entry stops describing a divergence and the checker will demand its removal - which is the property that stops this line becoming permanent.

.views > .view.hero, .comp > .view.hero.why: OUR LANDMARK, NOT A #575 RE-SCOPING, and round three mislabelled it. The spec has this as `.comp > .view.hero`. Our four views sit inside a `<main class="views">` landmark rather than directly in `.comp`, so the design's child combinator matched nothing at all and computed padding-top 0. The selector carries BOTH spellings so the rule applies in our structure and still describes the design's. Same declarations as the spec - verified - but the reason is the landmark, and globals.css has nothing to do with it.

html[data-theme].why:
RE-SCOPED TO OUTRANK globals.css, AND IT ADDS ONE DECLARATION, NAMED. The re-scoping is as above - one ancestor, so it outranks the legacy sheet. What it adds beyond the design's body is:
  background:var(--page)
which closes globals.css:72 `html { background: var(--color-bg); }`. globals paints the root with the OLD palette and nothing in the transcription names html's background, so the overscroll and rubber-band area behind the page kept the pre-redesign colour while the page itself was on --page. Only visible on a bounce, which is why nobody would find it by looking. The attribute selector is what outranks the bare `html`.
Named per the CTO's round-three ruling: an `override` whose body adds to the spec's names each addition and the globals.css rule it closes, or it is a `divergence`. Round three pasted "SAME DECLARATIONS" onto this entry and it was false - the checker's own sameBodies says so.

.tabs button.why:
THE UNSELECTED TAB DID NOT READ AS A CONTROL. The design gives it `border: .06u solid var(--hair)`, and --hair is #efe6df against a #fff surface: a contrast ratio of 1.23:1, which is a hairline you cannot see on a laptop screen. The selected tab is a filled ink pill, so the pair read as 'a label, and some grey text beside it' rather than as two tabs - the owner reported exactly that, unprompted, from a screenshot. A control whose affordance depends on the viewer already knowing it is a control is not a control.

Raised to --prompt-border, #beb4ae, 2.03:1. NOT an invented colour: it is the token the design itself puts on `.prompt`, the address input - the border it already uses to say 'this is an interactive edge'. So the change borrows the design's own vocabulary rather than departing from its palette, and the two interactive boxes in the card now agree with each other.

Still a departure, because the snapshot is a static mock where nothing is ever pressed and the unselected state only has to look quiet. It is the same family as the tap floor: the preview is not wrong, it is answering a question a live page has to answer differently.
